claims.text: Thermal activation transforms an initially non-equilibrium, supersaturated solid solution into a phase-separated composite microstructure.
The phase-separated microstructure contains discrete Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Phase separation promotes a more adherent and protective high-temperature oxide scale.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates create local galvanic couples that accelerate localized aqueous corrosion.
The initial alloy is an as-cast, homogeneous, supersaturated solid solution.
The initial alloy has a density below 6 g/cm³.
An isothermal aging treatment at 300–500 °C can trigger phase separation.
Aging must provide sufficient atomic mobility without melting for the proposed transformation to occur.
Aging forms fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates within the remaining matrix.
Mg-rich intermetallic formation alters the local elemental distribution at the alloy surface.
Surface segregation caused by Mg-rich intermetallics facilitates formation of a thicker, more adherent oxide scale.
The thicker, more adherent oxide scale improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Chemical heterogeneity between intermetallic precipitates and the matrix establishes galvanic couples.
Galvanic coupling between precipitates and the matrix accelerates localized corrosion.
Aged samples will show lower oxidation-induced weight gain than as-cast samples.
Aged samples will show greater localized corrosion, including higher corrosion current density, than as-cast samples.
The as-cast baseline has a homogeneous elemental distribution with minimal or no stable intermetallic phases.
The hypothesis is limited to Mg-containing high-entropy alloys with density below 6 g/cm³ for which moderate thermal aging is feasible.
